evidence_set: In all eight trials that described the time course, withdrawal signs and symptoms appeared earlier and resolved sooner with an alpha2 agonist; with tapered methadone, withdrawal in general peaked late, at the end of the taper.

Time in treatment shorter with an alpha2 agonist than with reducing doses of methadone: SMD -1.07 (-1.31 to -0.83), 3 trials, 310 participants, GRADE low; SMD -1.04 (-1.44 to -0.64) without the high-risk trial.

Hypotensive or other adverse effects, alpha2 agonist against reducing doses of methadone: RR 1.92 (1.19 to 3.10), 6 trials, 464 participants, GRADE low; illustrative 79 per 1000 with methadone against 151 per 1000 with an alpha2 agonist; without the three high-risk trials RR 2.02 (0.62 to 6.64), 203 participants. Drop-out for adverse effects RR 3.62 (0.77 to 16.94), 4 trials, 153 participants, no events in methadone arms. In one trial 89 of 100 people on clonidine had dizziness on standing.

Completion, alpha2 agonist against reducing doses of methadone: RR 0.85 (0.69 to 1.05), 9 trials, 659 participants, GRADE low (selection bias, heterogeneity); illustrative 568 per 1000 with methadone against 483 per 1000 with an alpha2 agonist; without San 1990 RR 0.91 (0.75 to 1.11). People withdrawing from heroin RR 0.87 (0.61 to 1.25); from methadone RR 0.97 (0.80 to 1.18); inpatient RR 0.87 (0.68 to 1.12), I2 67%; outpatient RR 1.09 (0.73 to 1.64).

Neither alpha2 agonists nor a methadone taper appeared to fully suppress aches and pains, sleep disturbance, loss of energy, chills or anxiety. The authors note that fixed methadone tapers in the trials, unlike flexible tapers in practice, would be expected to bias the comparison against methadone.

evidence_set: Completion of withdrawal treatment, buprenorphine against clonidine or lofexidine: RR 1.59 (95% CI 1.23 to 2.06), 11 trials (12 comparisons), 1264 participants, GRADE moderate (heterogeneity above 60%); illustrative 453 per 1000 with clonidine or lofexidine against 721 per 1000 with buprenorphine; number needed to treat for one additional completion 4 (2.8 to 6.7); inpatient RR 1.74 (1.05 to 2.89), 539 participants; outpatient RR 1.45 (1.12 to 1.88), 725 participants.

Mean overall withdrawal score lower with buprenorphine than with an alpha2 agonist in all seven trials reporting it: SMD -0.43 (-0.58 to -0.28), 902 participants, GRADE moderate (blinding of subjective outcomes); without four high-risk trials SMD -0.37 (-0.58 to -0.16).
Time in treatment longer with buprenorphine than with clonidine: SMD 0.92 (0.57 to 1.27), 4 trials (5 comparisons), 558 participants, GRADE moderate; large in both inpatient and outpatient settings.

Any adverse effect, buprenorphine against an alpha2 agonist: RR 0.93 (0.70 to 1.26), 3 trials (4 comparisons), 493 participants, GRADE very low; stopping for adverse effects only in clonidine arms, RR 0.20 (0.04 to 1.15), 3 inpatient trials, 134 participants, low. Dizziness, dry mouth and lethargy typical with clonidine; headache, constipation and nausea with buprenorphine.

evidence_set: Peak observer-rated withdrawal higher in the Fentanyl than in the Non-Fentanyl cohort from the second to the seventh day (F(1,6) = 7.76, p < 0.001). No participant reached moderately severe or severe COWS scores; mild observer-rated withdrawal, Fentanyl against Non-Fentanyl cohort, 73% against 33%, 70% against 13%, 73% against 18%, 60% against 15%, 53% against 18% and 40% against 14% on those days.

Tachycardia (heart rate above 100 at least once) in 43% of the Fentanyl cohort against 19% of the Non-Fentanyl cohort (p < 0.05); heart rate rose more steeply over the week in the Fentanyl than in the Non-Fentanyl cohort (interaction p = 0.007).
Methods › Measures, 2nd paragraph; Results › Physiological Measures › Heart Rate, 1st paragraph

The Fentanyl cohort was older than the Non-Fentanyl cohort (mean 46.0, SD 10.1, against 41.2, SD 10.2; p = 0.021). Concomitant medicines for withdrawal symptoms were available during stabilization only in the Fentanyl trial, because of uncontrolled withdrawal.
